question:
A company is evaluating Microsoft Fabric as its analytics platform.

Which three statements about Microsoft Fabric are true? (Choose 3)

options.text: It is a unified software-as-a-service analytics platform that brings data integration, data engineering, warehousing, real-time analytics, data science, and business intelligence together
Its items — such as lakehouses, warehouses, pipelines, and reports — are created and organized in workspaces
Its different workloads can operate on the same stored copy of data, rather than each workload keeping its own separate copy
Customers must provision, size, and patch their own Spark clusters and virtual machines before using it
It can process only streaming data, so batch analytics still requires a separate platform

explanation:
Microsoft Fabric's defining traits:
- **Unified SaaS platform** — Fabric packages the full analytics estate — Data Factory-style integration, Spark-based engineering, warehousing, real-time intelligence, data science, and Power BI — as one software-as-a-service offering with shared governance and capacity.
- **Workspaces** — Everything you build in Fabric (lakehouses, warehouses, pipelines, semantic models, reports) is an item that lives in a workspace, which organizes content and controls collaboration and access.
- **One copy of data across workloads** — Fabric's workloads share a common storage foundation, so a Spark notebook, a SQL endpoint, and a Power BI model can all work against the same stored tables instead of each engine hoarding its own duplicate.

**Why not the other options:**
- **Provisioning and patching Spark clusters and VMs** — As a SaaS platform, Fabric supplies the compute behind every experience; there is no customer-managed cluster or VM to size or patch.
- **Streaming only** — Fabric handles batch pipelines, warehouse loads, and scheduled transformations alongside its real-time capabilities; it is a general analytics platform, not a streaming-only tool.
category: Describe an Analytics Workload on Azure
